message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Parallel graphics rendering – originally for drawing pixels on screen, now also used for massively parallel compute tasks. |
| **Core count** | Few cores (typically 2–32 in consumer CPUs). | Hundreds or thousands of smaller cores (e.g., 1,000+ in modern GPUs). |
| **Execution style** | Serial or low‑parallelism; each core can handle complex branching and large caches. | SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) – many cores execute the same instruction on different data simultaneously. |
| **Cache hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, optimized for random access patterns. | Smaller per‑core caches; relies on high memory bandwidth and coalesced accesses. |
| **Clock speed** | Higher clock speeds (often >3 GHz) because fewer cores and more complex pipelines. | Lower clock speeds (often <1 GHz) because many cores share resources. |
| **Instruction set** | Complex, rich instruction sets (x86, ARM) with branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution. | Simpler, highly parallel instruction sets (CUDA, OpenCL, Vulkan). |
| **Typical workloads** | Single‑threaded or lightly threaded tasks, heavy branching, I/O bound operations. | Highly parallel tasks like matrix multiplication, image processing, machine learning inference/training, scientific simulations. |
| **Memory access pattern** | Random, unpredictable; benefits from large caches and sophisticated prefetchers. | Structured, predictable; benefits from wide memory buses and burst transfers. |
| **Energy efficiency** | Optimized for performance per watt in serial workloads. | Optimized for throughput per watt in parallel workloads. |

### Why the difference matters

- **Parallelism**: A GPU’s many cores excel when you can split a problem into thousands of independent threads. A CPU’s few cores are better when each thread needs to make many decisions or access diverse data.
- **Latency vs. throughput**: CPUs minimize latency for individual instructions; GPUs maximize throughput for batches of identical operations.
- **Programming model**: CPUs use general-purpose languages (C/C++, Java, etc.) and rely on the OS scheduler. GPUs require specialized APIs (CUDA, OpenCL, DirectX, Vulkan) and explicit memory management.

In practice, most modern systems combine both: the CPU handles control flow, system services, and tasks that don’t parallelize well, while the GPU accelerates compute‑heavy, data‑parallel workloads. This synergy is why GPUs have become popular not only for gaming but also for AI training, scientific computing, and even general‑purpose GPU computing (GPGPU).
